entities.summary:
Juan de Borja Lanzol de Romaní, known as "the Younger" to distinguish him from an older cousin of the same name, emerged as a prominent Spanish Roman Catholic cardinal and archbishop during the late 15th century, a period marked by intense political maneuvering and ecclesiastical ambition within the Renaissance Papacy. Born around 1470 into the powerful Borja family of Valencia, his rapid ascent through the Church hierarchy was directly facilitated by his uncle, Rodrigo Borgia, who became Pope Alexander VI in 1492. Juan's career epitomized the pervasive nepotism and pluralism characteristic of the era, reflecting the Borgia family's strategic consolidation of power and wealth through ecclesiastical appointments. His brief but impactful life, culminating in his death in 1500, underscores the volatile dynamics of the papal court and the intricate web of familial alliances that shaped European politics and religion.

Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Alexander VI on February 19, 1496, Juan de Borja Lanzol de Romaní became Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata and subsequently held the prestigious Archbishops of Monreale in Sicily (from 1496) and Bishop of Melfi (from 1494). These appointments, often held concurrently, provided substantial income and influence, allowing him to serve as a key administrative and diplomatic agent for his papal uncle. He participated actively in the Curia, undertaking various legatine missions, including a significant assignment to Perugia and Cagli in 1497 to restore order and assert papal authority. His ecclesiastical career, though cut short, was a testament to the Borgia family's effective use of the Church's institutional framework to advance its temporal objectives.
